summary: A superconducting qubit array coupled to a common microwave waveguide enables programmable control of collective dissipation with simultaneous access to microscopic many-body dynamics. Site-resolved measurements reveal how strong coherent interactions reshape superradiant and subradiant decay through spectrally structured many-body eigenstates, with tunable quantum correlations enabling exploration of collective phenomena beyond the ideal Dicke model.
motivation: Understanding microscopic many-body dynamics and quantum correlations during collective emission in regimes where coherent interactions compete with dissipation remains experimentally elusive, motivating development of platforms with simultaneous control over dissipation, interactions, and qubit-resolved measurements.
method: Four transmon qubits with nearest-neighbor exchange coupling $J \approx 2\pi \times 6$ MHz couple to resonators ($\kappa_r \approx 2\pi \times 1.5$ MHz) connected to a common waveguide. Parametric flux modulation engineers qubit-waveguide couplings with tunable amplitude ($\gamma_{\mathrm{wg}} \approx 2\pi \times 15$ kHz) and phase, enabling control of interference. Site-resolved control and readout track populations and two-qubit correlations throughout decay from prepared initial states across multiple excitation manifolds.
result: For uniform-phase coupling ($\theta = 0$), the highest-energy single-excitation eigenstate exhibits superradiant decay scaling linearly with lattice size ($\Gamma^{m=1} \approx \gamma_{\mathrm{wg}} N_q$), while decay from the fully inverted state shows non-exponential dynamics with enhanced emission rate $R(t) \approx 2\pi \times 130$ kHz during early superradiant regime ($t \lesssim 200$ ns), followed by long-lived subradiant tail ($t \sim 10$–$100$ µs). Transverse correlations develop with peak magnitude $C_{ij}^\perp \approx 0.15$ during superradiance and reverse sign during subradiance, demonstrating programmable spatial correlation patterns via phase engineering ($\theta = 0$ versus $\theta = \pi$).
